These small olive or reddish-brown insects feed on amaranths, often called pigweeds, and ants may attend their colonies. Their sheltered feeding sites can make them easy to miss during a quick look at the foliage. Similar aphids share these plants, so the host and body color alone do not confirm the species.

previousDescription: Amaranth aphids are small sap-feeding insects associated with amaranths, the plants often called pigweeds. This less visible feeding position is a useful part of their story: an apparently clean upper leaf does not describe the whole plant. Closely related aphids can look similar, so color and host name alone do not settle the identification.

Native to South America, it lives in floodplain waters and lagoons and is traded for aquariums as a pleco. Released or escaped fish have established populations elsewhere. Similar sailfin catfishes can interbreed, so markings alone do not always reveal which species an introduced fish belongs to.

Researchers have found self-sustaining stands along waterways and disturbed ground in parts of Southeast Asia. Closely related Cecropia species can look alike, making careful identification important when documenting new records.

Identifying the insect requires a close look at the beetle itself.

previousDescription: Anisandrus maiche is a tiny ambrosia beetle that spends much of its life out of sight inside wood. Females bore into woody plants and cultivate fungi in their tunnels; the fungi provide food for the developing young. Native to Asia, the species has also been documented in North America. Like other ambrosia beetles, it is easier to notice through its small entry holes than to identify by a casual look at the insect. Its partnership with fungi is central to its biology, and close examination is needed to separate it from similar wood-boring beetles.

proposedDescription: This ambrosia beetle is a small, slender, light-brown insect found in wood. Euwallacea similis has been recorded across parts of Asia and the Pacific, where it uses weakened trees and timber. Details on the ends of its wing covers help specialists distinguish it from related beetles. That distinction matters: the tree diseases and damage associated with other Euwallacea species should not automatically be attributed to this one.

previousDescription: Euwallacea similis is a small, slender ambrosia beetle that lives in wood. Its light brown body is a useful first clue, although separating it from similar beetles takes a close look at the wing covers. Believed native to the Asia-Pacific region and introduced elsewhere, it usually colonizes weakened or stressed trees and can damage stored timber in its tropical native range. Its presence deserves attention, but the severe tree diseases associated with other Euwallacea species should not automatically be attributed to this one.

proposedDescription: American evergreen is a familiar houseplant with arrow-shaped young leaves. As it grows and climbs, its leaves become more deeply divided. In warm places such as Florida, escaped plants can spread across the ground and climb trees, covering other vegetation. Pieces of stem can take root, so discarded garden material can help this tropical vine move beyond the place where it was planted.
researchNotes: Florida impacts are geographically bounded; indoor cultivation is not itself evidence of escape.
previousDescription: Arrowhead vine is the familiar tropical houseplant with pointed, arrow-shaped young leaves. Given warmth and something to climb, it becomes a much larger vine, and older leaves divide into several leaflets. Outside cultivation in southern Florida, it can blanket the ground, climb trees, and crowd native vegetation. Pieces discarded from gardens can take root, helping explain how an attractive indoor plant becomes a troublesome escape in warm natural areas.

proposedDescription: Caprella scaura looks more like a tiny walking stick than a shrimp. Its slender body and grasping limbs let it hold onto seaweed and the growth on docks, ropes and boat hulls. These surfaces also give it a way to travel between harbors. Where it becomes abundant, it can compete with other small marine animals for space and food, although its original native range remains uncertain.

previousDescription: Caprella scaura is a tiny marine crustacean known as a skeleton shrimp. Its long, sticklike body grips seaweeds and branching growth on docks, boats, and other submerged surfaces. That habit makes harbors useful places to look for it and gives it opportunities to travel with vessel fouling. Introduced populations can become very abundant and compete with other small crustaceans. Its original range remains uncertain, so records need to distinguish well-supported introductions from places with an unclear history.

proposedDescription: Amur corktree is a deciduous tree with deeply ridged bark and leaves made up of several leaflets. Female trees produce dark berries that can remain into winter, giving birds a meal and a way to spread the seeds. Introduced as an ornamental, it has established in parts of the northern United States. Its seedlings can grow beneath other trees, allowing it to enter forest understories.

previousDescription: Amur corktree is an Asian tree once planted for its broad crown and unusual, deeply ridged bark. Its leaves grow opposite one another and divide into several leaflets; female trees carry dark berries that may remain through winter. Birds spread the seeds beyond gardens, and seedlings tolerate forest shade. In parts of the northern United States, escaped trees can fill the understory and make it harder for native trees and other plants to regenerate.

proposedDescription: Amur goby is a small East Asian fish that lives close to the bottom of streams and other waters. Its slender body, fused pelvic-fin disc and red stripe from the eye toward the snout are useful clues. Modern research has confirmed Rhinogobius brunneus in Japan and southeastern Korea. The name historically covered several related fishes, however, so older northwestern U.S. records should not automatically be assigned to this narrowly defined species.

Its leaves appear early and linger late, giving the shrub a long season to shade the ground and suppress native wildflowers and tree seedlings.

proposedDescription: Anchorworm is a crustacean, despite its wormlike appearance. The adult female attaches to a fish with an anchor-shaped structure embedded in its skin, leaving much of her long body exposed. It affects fish including carp, koi and goldfish, especially in warm water. Attachment sites can become wounds, and heavy infestations can weaken fish. Moving infested fish can introduce the parasite to new ponds.

The adult female becomes a slender, wormlike strand attached to a fish, with an anchor-shaped head buried in its tissue. Carp, goldfish, koi, and many other freshwater fishes can host it, especially in warm ponds. Feeding and attachment wounds can weaken fish and, in heavy infestations, contribute to serious disease. Visible strands need careful identification because other fish parasites can look similar.

proposedDescription: Angel's-wings is a cactus whose paired, oval pads often resemble rabbit ears. The pads carry clusters of tiny, barbed bristles rather than the obvious long spines of many other cacti; these bristles can irritate skin. Yellow flowers may be followed by purple fruit. Popular in pots and dry gardens, it can spread from fallen pads where conditions suit it. Dense invasive stands are documented in Australia; those impacts should be distinguished from its status at a particular U.S. location.

proposedDescription: Angleton bluestem is a warm-season perennial grass grown for forage. It forms upright clumps with several narrow flowering branches spreading from near the top of each stem. It grows in upright clumps and carries several slender, fingerlike flowering branches near the top of each stem. Hairs around the flowering branches help botanists distinguish it from related bluestems, which can be difficult to separate at a glance. Its history connects pasture planting with establishment beyond cultivation; a record of the grass does not, by itself, show that native vegetation is being displaced.

proposedDescription: Angoumois grain moth spends its most damaging stage hidden inside a grain kernel. Its larvae feed within crops such as wheat and corn, including grain in storage. Adults are small, pale moths with narrow, fringed wings and do not feed. Because the larvae are concealed, infested grain may look largely intact until a moth emerges through a small hole.

Its caterpillars bore into kernels of wheat, corn, and other cereals, feeding and developing there before the adults emerge. Adult moths have narrow, fringed wings and do not feed. Infestation can begin in a crop and continue in storage, reducing the quantity and quality of grain. Because the larvae live inside individual kernels, an apparently tidy grain surface can conceal the problem.

Despite its name, it produces seed and has traveled widely beyond its native Mediterranean and neighboring regions. It occurs in fields and other disturbed places and can contaminate harvested seed. It also has value to crop breeders, who use wild-oat diversity as a source of useful traits, including disease resistance.

proposedDescription: Anise, listed here as Myrrhis odorata, is a perennial herb with finely divided leaves, clusters of small white flowers and a strong anise-like scent. Long grown as a culinary herb, it has escaped cultivation in parts of North America. It has finely divided foliage and small white flowers gathered into umbrella-shaped clusters. Garden escapes sometimes turn up in disturbed ground in North America. The familiar common name can cause confusion because unrelated native American plants are also called sweet cicely. previousDescription: Annual mercury is a branching plant with toothed green leaves and small, inconspicuous flowers. Male flowers are held on narrow spikes, while female flowers sit closer to the leaf joints, often on separate plants. It grows in cultivated and disturbed ground and completes its life cycle in one season. The flower arrangement is more useful for identification than its otherwise fairly ordinary green leaves.

proposedDescription: Annual rabbitsfootgrass gets its name from its soft-looking, fuzzy flower heads. The dense clusters are pale green at first and turn straw-colored as they mature, with fine bristles giving them their distinctive texture. It commonly grows in damp, disturbed places such as ditches, pond margins and irrigated fields. Although it may form thick patches, it is an annual that returns from seed.

researchNotes: Both full pages opened. UC supports habitats and weed relevance; Flora independently supports morphology. No generalized wetland-damage claim.
previousDescription: Rabbitfoot grass gets its name from its soft-looking, densely packed flower head. The pale green head becomes straw-colored as it matures, with fine bristles giving it a fuzzy outline. This annual grass often grows where soil stays damp, including ditches, pond edges, and irrigated fields. It can become a weed in crops, lawns, and other managed ground. Moisture and the mature flower head are useful clues, although a confirmed identification still matters where similar grasses grow together.

proposedDescription: Annual ryegrass is a fast-growing grass used for forage and cover crops. Its glossy leaves clasp the stem, and its seeds develop along a narrow spike, often with bristles projecting from the flower clusters. It can also become a troublesome weed in grain fields. Despite the name, some plants live into a second season, and closely related ryegrasses can be difficult to tell apart.

previousDescription: Italian ryegrass is a fast-growing grass used for forage, cover crops, and temporary green cover. Its glossy leaves clasp the stem at their bases, and the flowering spike carries rows of small spikelets, often with slender awns. It usually behaves as an annual or biennial. The same vigorous growth that makes it useful in cultivation can make escaped plants difficult weeds in grain crops. Its role depends on context: a deliberately planted crop and an unwanted population are not the same thing.

proposedDescription: Annual wallrocket begins with a cluster of toothed leaves near the ground. Slender, mostly leafless stems rise above them and carry small yellow flowers with four petals. It grows in disturbed places, including paths, field margins and around walls. Originally from parts of Europe and nearby regions, it has been introduced to North America, where it can resemble several other small mustard-family weeds.

Slender stems rise above it with relatively few leaves and small four-petaled flowers. Originally from Europe and neighboring regions, it now occurs widely beyond that range, including North America. Disturbed ground and wall margins are characteristic places to find it. Its presence documents an introduced plant; the sources reviewed do not justify treating every occurrence as a damaging invasion.

proposedDescription: Annual yellow sweetclover has leaves divided into three leaflets and narrow clusters of tiny yellow flowers. These develop into small, rounded pods with visible veins. It grows in disturbed ground and cultivated settings, including orchards, vineyards and grain fields. Its modest flower size helps distinguish it from larger sweetclovers, though a close look at the pods is often useful.

Its small flowers help distinguish it from larger sweetclovers, though the group can be confusing. A record is most useful when it identifies this species accurately rather than borrowing the impacts of a different sweetclover.

proposedDescription: Myzaphis rosarum is a small yellow-green aphid found on roses and shrubby cinquefoil. It often feeds along the midribs of young leaves, on either surface. Its short antennae and the shape of the tubes at the rear are useful features under magnification. Winged and wingless forms differ, and related aphids can look similar, so the host plant and close examination are more useful than color alone.

previousDescription: Myzaphis rosarum is a tiny yellow to green aphid found on roses and shrubby cinquefoil. It often feeds along veins on young or unfolding leaves. Short antennae and slightly swollen tubes at the rear of the body help distinguish it under magnification. It is less often associated with severe outbreaks than some familiar rose aphids, though its small size can make colonies easy to overlook.

proposedDescription: Myzus varians feeds beneath peach leaves, which may roll tightly lengthwise and turn reddish around its colonies. Wingless adults are pale green; winged adults are darker. In its seasonal cycle it can move between peach and clematis, overwintering as eggs near peach buds. Experiments have shown that it can carry plum pox virus from peach to clematis. Finding the aphid or a curled leaf alone does not confirm that a plant is infected.

An independent Arzone/Alma field-study abstract was also read as corroborative context but not needed to inflate source count.

The species can transmit plum pox virus, but its presence alone does not establish that a tree is infected. Both insect identification and plant diagnosis require more than curled leaves.

proposedDescription: Pleotrichophorus chrysanthemi is a pale yellow-green aphid found beneath chrysanthemum leaves. Feeding may be associated with yellowing, including on plants grown under greenhouse conditions. Its identity is complicated by questions about how it differs from the closely related P. glandulosus. Specialists compare tiny body hairs and other structures, together with the host plant. A careful identification is therefore important before treating similar aphids on chrysanthemums as the same species.

proposedDescription: Rhopalomyzus lonicerae has different-looking colonies at different points in its life cycle. Dark green aphids feed on honeysuckle in spring, where leaves may roll around them. Later, paler colonies can occur on grasses, including reed canarygrass in wet places. This seasonal change in host and appearance is useful context: two colonies that look different may still belong to the same species.

previousDescription: Rhopalomyzus lonicerae is an aphid whose appearance changes with its seasonal hosts. On honeysuckle in spring, dark green colonies can roll and discolor young leaves. Later generations move to grasses, especially reed canarygrass, where much paler colonies can become abundant along waterways. An entomologist's western U.S. field observations document both sides of that cycle. Knowing the host connection helps explain why insects on a garden shrub and nearby grass may belong to the same species, without assuming that every colony causes lasting damage.

proposedDescription: Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale is commonly associated with roots, where its colonies are easily missed. The aphids are greenish to brown, sometimes with a rusty area toward the rear, and use grasses and other plants, including greenhouse crops. Their hidden feeding habits can complicate diagnosis. Poor root growth alone is not enough to identify them; the insects themselves need to be found and examined.

Existing speciesId preserved; preferred scientific spelling in the sources is rufiabdominale.

proposedDescription: Sipha glyceriae is a tiny aphid most often found on grasses in damp places, with some records from sedges and rushes too. Wingless adults are usually dull green, sometimes reddish, and may have a paler stripe along the back. They are only about two millimeters long. Unlike aphids that move between trees and grasses through the seasons, this species completes its cycle on herbaceous plants. Identifying it confidently requires a close look: specialists compare its body hairs and minute surface features with those of related grass aphids.

It corroborates the wet-grass habitat, occasional sedge/rush hosts, dull-green color and small size and supplies original diagnostic hair/cuticle characters. Stroyan acknowledges museum access from Eastop, but this is a separately authored specimen-based key, not a mirror or republication of their web synthesis. No damage severity or control advice is inferred.
previousDescription: Sipha glyceriae is an aphid of wet places, feeding on grasses, rushes and sedges. Its green body may show a reddish stripe and lighter markings along the back. It uses herbaceous hosts through its seasonal cycle rather than relying on an obvious tree-to-grass migration. Looking closely at wetland vegetation can reveal colonies that would otherwise blend into their surroundings.

Wetland grasses and records from rushes/sedges
Monoecious holocyclic life cycle
S. glyceriae classified as adventive in North America

proposedDescription: Sipha maydis is a dark, glossy aphid with stiff hairs, often found near the bases of grass leaves. It feeds on grasses and cereal crops, including wheat, barley, oats and corn. Colonies can injure leaves, and the species can also transmit plant viruses. Its nearly black or brown appearance helps distinguish it from some common green aphids, though a close examination is still important.
identification: Look for 1-2 mm dark, hairy aphids where the leaf meets the stem; confirm with a cereal-aphid key.
actions: Photograph the colony and its host, and ask agricultural extension to confirm the species if crop injury is developing.

previousDescription: A patch of dark specks near the base of a grass leaf can turn out to be a colony of hedgehog grain aphids. Sipha maydis feeds on cereals and other grasses, including wheat, barley, oats, and corn. Unlike many green cereal aphids, its wingless adults are glossy brown-black and covered with stiff hairs. Feeding colonies can injure leaves, and the species has been reported as a grass-virus vector. It is an introduced aphid in North America, but a field sighting still needs identification before a crop-management decision.

proposedDescription: Tinocallis ulmiparvifoliae is an aphid associated with Chinese elm. Winged individuals have pale blue-green bodies with white wax stripes and spots, and colonies feed on the leaves. Originally associated with Asia, it has also been recorded in Florida as an introduced insect. Its host is a useful clue, but fine anatomical features are needed to distinguish it confidently from other elm-feeding aphids.
identification: Record the elm species and obtain a close photograph of the winged insects; wax and wing markings need specialist comparison.

Originally associated with Asia, it has also been recorded in Florida as an introduced insect. Its host is a useful clue, but fine anatomical features are needed to distinguish it confidently from other elm-feeding aphids.

proposedDescription: Tuberocephalus sakurae is a tiny aphid associated with cherry trees. Feeding can turn the leaves red or yellow and curl them into sheltered spaces for the insects. Wingless adults on cherry are dark green to black, with brighter young nearby. The species also alternates to underground parts of Artemisia plants. Distorted leaves may be easier to notice than the aphids themselves, but similar damage can have other causes and does not establish the species on its own.
identification: Inspect the inside of reddened, curled cherry leaves and record the host tree; symptoms alone are not a species diagnosis.

Research from Japan describes individuals only around a millimeter and a half long. The altered leaves may be easier to notice than the aphids themselves, but similar damage can have other causes and does not establish the species on its own.

proposedDescription: Uroleucon picridis is a shiny reddish-brown aphid associated with oxtongues in the genus Picris. Colonies may gather on stems just below the flowers. Dark antennae and rear tubes contrast with a paler, yellowish tail-like projection at the end of the body. These details help specialists distinguish it from related aphids. Host identification matters too: some older records from other plants involve similar species, so color alone is not enough for a reliable identification.
identification: Compare a close view of the aphid with the flowering host; color alone will not separate related Uroleucon.

proposedDescription: This aphid parasite is a tiny wasp that uses aphids as a nursery for its young. A female Aphidius ervi lays an egg inside an aphid; the developing wasp eventually leaves a dry, swollen shell called a mummy and emerges through a round hole. It attacks aphids including potato and foxglove aphids and is used in biological control. Its presence can therefore reflect pest management rather than a new pest problem.
identification: Look for aphid mummies and circular emergence holes; these indicate parasitoid activity but do not identify the wasp species on their own.
actions: When managing aphids, check for mummies and other natural enemies. Match any planned biological-control release to the aphid species with greenhouse or extension guidance.

previousDescription: A swollen, papery-looking aphid can be the sign that a tiny wasp is doing useful work. Aphidius ervi lays an egg inside an aphid; the growing wasp develops there and eventually leaves through a round hole in the resulting aphid mummy. Adults are slender black wasps with long antennae. Growers use this species as a biological control agent, particularly against larger aphids such as potato and foxglove aphids. Its presence deserves a different response from that of a crop pest: the wasp is part of the community that can help suppress aphids.

proposedDescription: Apple aphid gathers on young leaves and shoots, including the vigorous upright shoots of apple trees. The green insects feed on plant sap and produce sticky honeydew that can support sooty mold. Heavy colonies may weaken young growth, while predators can help limit their numbers. The aphid survives winter as dark eggs on woody growth, ready to hatch as fresh leaves become available.
identification: Green aphids with dark rear tubes on tender apple growth resemble spirea aphids; glossy black winter eggs are not unique to this species.
actions: Monitor infested shoots and natural enemies, especially on young trees. Use local orchard or extension guidance if colonies are causing sustained injury.

previousDescription: Green apple aphids gather where an apple tree is growing fastest: tender shoot tips, young leaves, and water sprouts. Their small green bodies can be easy to miss until leaves curl or sticky honeydew appears. In heavy colonies, that honeydew supports dark sooty mold on foliage and fruit, and feeding can slow young trees. The aphids overwinter as black eggs on woody growth. Lady beetles, lacewings, and other predators often keep them in check, so noticing aphids is a reason to inspect the whole shoot, including its natural enemies, before deciding what to do.

proposedDescription: Apple blossom, Cassia javanica, is a tropical tree grown for generous clusters of pink flowers. Its leaves are divided into pairs of leaflets, and its fruit develops into long, cylindrical pods. The tree has a spreading crown and can lose some or all of its leaves seasonally. Several botanical forms differ in their leaves and flower clusters, so a precise identification benefits from photographs of both. Despite its common name, it belongs to the legume family.
identification: Photograph a complete leaf, flowers, and pods; identification below species level may require stipule and sepal details.

Its leaves are divided into pairs of leaflets, and its fruit develops into long, cylindrical pods. Different forms within the species vary in appearance, which can complicate identification. The common name refers to the flowers' ornamental appeal; this is a member of the legume family, not an apple tree.

It has paired leaflets and pink flowers, with branching flower clusters at the ends of young leafy shoots. Pink flowers alone cannot separate it from related forms. A comparative study identifies leaflet details, shoot hairs, stipules and flower structures as useful clues, so a confident identification needs a closer look than flower color.

proposedDescription: Apple mealybug is a soft-bodied insect covered in white wax. It feeds on several woody plants, not just apples, and may hide in bark crevices where colonies are easy to miss. White egg sacs and sticky honeydew can reveal its presence. It is also a known vector of little cherry virus 2, making accurate identification particularly important in affected fruit-growing areas.
identification: Look for oval wax-covered insects and white egg sacs; distinguish them from the longer woolly coating of woolly apple aphids.
actions: Have suspected orchard infestations identified, especially near cherries. Ask local tree-fruit extension about monitoring when little cherry disease is a concern.

previousDescription: Apple mealybugs often announce themselves as little patches of white wax on a tree. Beneath that powdery covering is a soft oval insect; mature females produce conspicuous white egg sacs. The species uses a range of woody hosts, and in orchards its honeydew can leave fruit and foliage sticky and encourage sooty mold. Mealybugs can also shelter in protected parts of a tree, making a quick glance at the leaves an incomplete inspection. Apple mealybug matters particularly in cherry production because it is associated with transmission of little cherry virus 2.

proposedDescription: Applemint is a perennial herb with rounded, wrinkled, hairy leaves and a fruity scent. Small, pale flowers grow in spikes above the foliage. It spreads through underground stems, which can carry it beyond the edges of a garden bed. Native to parts of Europe and the Mediterranean region, it also grows outside cultivation in moist ground. Its soft leaves help distinguish it from smoother-leaved mints.
identification: Look for softly hairy, toothed, rounded leaves and dense pale flower spikes; scent supports identification but is not sufficient on its own.
actions: Contain a garden planting and check for shoots escaping its boundary. RHS recommends deep containers to limit spread.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: Mentha suaveolens

previousDescription: Apple mint brings a fruity mint scent and soft, rounded leaves to herb gardens. The leaves are hairy and wrinkled, and pale flower spikes rise above the patch in summer. This is a creeping perennial: underground stems let a small planting expand steadily into neighboring ground, especially where conditions stay moist. That vigor is useful in a contained planting but can become a nuisance in an open bed. Native to parts of Europe and the Mediterranean region, it has been grown and naturalized elsewhere; garden spread should be described separately from documented ecological harm.

proposedDescription: Apple of Peru has pale blue, bell-shaped flowers followed by fruit enclosed in a papery covering. This annual member of the nightshade family comes from South America and can grow quickly in fertile, disturbed ground. It spreads by seed and may appear as a garden escape or field weed. Despite the familiar-looking fruit covering, it should not be confused with edible groundcherries.
identification: Look for angular stems, broad unevenly toothed or lobed leaves, blue flowers with pale centers, and inflated fruit coverings.
actions: Avoid eating the fruits or other plant parts. If removing unwanted plants, act before mature seed is shed.

previousDescription: Apple of Peru looks at home in a flower border, with pale blue bells and a papery case around each fruit. It is a summer annual in the nightshade family, native to South America and naturalized in parts of the United States. Plants grow quickly in disturbed, fertile ground and spread by abundant seed. That combination has carried this ornamental into crop fields and other disturbed sites. Its lanternlike fruits can suggest an edible ground cherry, but the resemblance is misleading: this plant should not be treated as a food plant.

proposedDescription: Arabian jasmine is an evergreen shrub or scrambling climber with glossy, oval leaves and strongly scented white flowers. The flowers may turn pink as they age, and cultivated forms can have one or several layers of petals. Despite its name, its native range includes areas from Bhutan to India. It is widely grown in warm climates for its flowers and fragrance.
identification: Compare the glossy, simple leaves and fragrant white flowers; doubled cultivars can obscure normal flower structure.

previousDescription: Arabian jasmine is best known for the fragrance of its white flowers. This evergreen shrub can scramble over nearby support, carrying glossy oval leaves and blooms that may blush pink as they age. Cultivated forms range from simple flowers to richly doubled rosettes, so a garden specimen may look quite different from another plant of the same species. Despite its common name, Kew places its native range in Bhutan and India. Its long history in gardens and flower use is part of its story, but does not by itself demonstrate ecological harm where it has been introduced.

proposedDescription: Arabian schismus is a small annual grass with fine leaves and a short, compact flower head. It grows in dry, open places and disturbed desert ground. In the southwestern United States, its dried growth can help carry fire across spaces between shrubs, especially when seasons of abundant rain produce more vegetation. It closely resembles Schismus barbatus, another introduced desert grass. Small differences in the flower parts are more dependable for separating them than a photograph of their leaves.
identification: Examine mature flower parts with a regional grass key; a photograph of fine leaves alone is not reliable.

previousDescription: Arabian schismus is a small annual grass that grows in dry, open places. After rain, its fine leaves and stems can fill spaces between desert shrubs; when dry, that growth can help fire move through areas that once had little continuous fuel. It closely resembles another introduced schismus grass, so small flower details are important for separating the two species.

Disturbed/desert habitat; similarity to S. barbatus; both carry fire between shrubs in California desert.
34-site fuels study and three burn sites; both Schismus species dominant/codominant in some sites; winter rain 200% normal and persistent dead annual grasses.

proposedDescription: Brachyrhynchus membranaceus is a flat bug associated with fungi and decaying wood. Its flattened body suits the sheltered spaces used by these insects. Originally known from the Old World, it has also been documented in the Caribbean and Central America. It feeds on fungal growth and has sometimes damaged cultivated bracket fungi. Finding this insect around wood does not by itself show that a healthy tree is being attacked; its documented food is fungal tissue.
identification: A flattened brown bug around fungus-bearing wood needs expert comparison with other flat bugs.

sources.title: USDA ARS: Henry et al. 2013 Brachyrhynchus membranaceus
Taszakowski and Kaszyca-Taszakowska 2020: Teratological cases of antennae in Aradidae

researchNotes: USDA interpretive summary and technical abstract now read in full, recovering prior missing feeding evidence. Independent full microscopy paper read, including exact species results and Figure 5 caption. Habitat explanation is family context corroborating the species' fungal association, not evidence of universal tree harmlessness. Microscopy findings substantiate identification complexity but do not imply ecological impact.
previousDescription: This aradid flat bug lives around decaying wood and feeds on fungi. Its flattened body suits the narrow spaces beneath bark and within woody material. Brachyrhynchus membranaceus has records in both the Old World and the Western Hemisphere, and has sometimes affected cultivated bracket fungi. Finding it in wood does not mean it is attacking a healthy tree; its feeding is associated with fungal growth.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Henry et al 2013 New World study
supportedClaims: Fungal mycelium feeding; damage to cultivated medicinal bracket fungi; established New World populations; flattened aradid body.
Examined B. membranaceus male; normal four-segment antenna versus regenerated three-segment antenna; microscopic sensory structures; aradid decaying-wood habitat context.

proposedDescription: Araucaria aphid feeds on young growth of Araucaria trees, including around the bases of needles on fresh shoots. Wingless individuals are broadly oval and bright yellow to orange, measuring only about one to one and a half millimeters long. Their tiny size makes a close look worthwhile. The species has been recorded in several tropical and subtropical regions, but that wide distribution does not clearly identify its original home. The host and color are useful clues rather than a complete diagnosis.
identification: Check fresh Araucaria shoots for broad yellow to orange aphids; confirm with a specialist rather than relying on color.

sources.title: Noordam 2004: Aphids of Java Part VI

researchNotes: Noordam original living-material description and specialist synthesis now read. They represent separate Java observations and Carver-based regional interpretation, even though synthesis cites Noordam among genus references. Native origin remains explicitly uncertain; not a blocking gap for the bounded biological description.
previousDescription: Araucaria aphid feeds on young growth of Araucaria trees. Wingless individuals are broadly oval and yellow to orange, measuring only around one to one and a half millimeters long. It has been recorded in tropical regions where its host trees grow. Its small size makes close examination useful, and its wider distribution should not be treated as a clear map of its original native range.

supportedClaims: Broad yellow-orange wingless adults 1.1–1.5 mm; young Araucaria growth; uncertain native origin.
Pages 124–125: collected on Araucaria cunninghamii; yellow body, pale appendages; feeding at needle bases on young shoots; morphology key.

proposedDescription: Araucaria black scale can look like a dark speck attached to a leaf. The female shelters beneath a nearly circular, flattened brown-black cover with darker shed skins near its center. Despite the name, its hosts extend well beyond Araucaria: palms, olives and many other woody plants have been recorded. This broad host range makes examination of the insect especially useful. A dark spot on a familiar plant can suggest an armored scale, but it does not establish this species.
identification: Inspect dark circular leaf scales with magnification; an adult female may need slide-mounted examination.

sources.title: Bjelis et al. 2024: status of Lindingaspis rossi in Croatia

researchNotes: Exact ScaleNet structure passage and independent original field-survey abstract read. ScaleNet includes the 2024 paper in host lists; independence rests on its Ferris morphology versus new Croatian observations, not on duplicate host records. Publication title prints 1989 whereas taxonomic sources give 1891/1892; preserve species ID and omit author-year rather than propagate the typo.
previousDescription: Araucaria black scale forms a small, round, dark covering on its host plant. The cover is usually brown to black, with darker remains of earlier skins near the center. Despite the name, it can feed on plants beyond Araucaria. Like other armored scales, the insect spends much of its life protected beneath this cover, making the covering more visible than the animal itself.

supportedClaims: Flat circular dark female cover, near-central exuviae; leaf occurrence; historical broad host records.
20 plant species in 14 families confirmed hosts; Phoenix canariensis and Olea europaea prominent; restricted Croatian establishment.

proposedDescription: Arborescent pricklypear is a Mexican cactus that can grow into a large shrub or small tree. Its gray-green pads carry white hairs and spines, while older growth develops a trunk. Yellow flowers are followed by fleshy fruit. Broken pads can take root, allowing plants to spread from discarded garden material. It has escaped cultivation in places including Australia, where dense growth can become a management problem.
identification: Look for a trunked habit, finely hairy pads, and slender white spines; compare with similar prickly pears.
actions: Avoid spreading detached pads or dumping cactus material in natural areas. Use local disposal guidance and protect hands from spines and tiny barbed glochids.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Opuntia leucotricha
NSW Department of Primary Industries: Aaron's beard prickly pear

researchNotes: NSW Flora diagnostic description and NSW WeedWise biology, spread and management passages read. Australian escape and spread context is explicit; no U.S. regulatory status inferred.
previousDescription: Aaron's beard prickly pear can grow from a cluster of pads into a branching, trunked shrub. Its gray-green pads carry tiny pale hairs and flexible white spines, while yellow flowers are followed by fleshy fruit. Native to Mexico, it has escaped cultivation in parts of Australia, where managers document spread from detached plant pieces and dumped garden material. Those Australian impacts should not be assumed everywhere, but the way the plant travels is useful to understand. A broken pad can be more than waste: it may be the start of another plant.

proposedDescription: Argentine ants are small brown ants often seen moving in long, busy trails. They form networks of shallow nests with multiple queens and can spread through gardens, buildings and natural areas. Native to South America, they have become established in many other regions. They collect sugary honeydew from sap-feeding insects and can displace other ants where their colonies become dominant.
identification: Workers are uniformly dull brown, about 1/8 inch long, with one waist node; confirm against other small household ants.
actions: Follow trails to locate entry points and nests, confirm the ant, and use local species-appropriate bait guidance if control is needed.

sources.title: University of California IPM: Argentine Ant

researchNotes: UC IPM identification account and Texas A&M biology and management account read. Bait advice is conditional on confirmed identification; no blanket outdoor spraying advice.
previousDescription: A busy ribbon of small brown ants along a wall or garden path may belong to Argentine ants. Workers are similar in size and move between shallow nests that can form part of a much larger network with many queens. Originally South American, this ant has become established in other regions and readily uses gardens and buildings. It feeds on sweet foods and tends honeydew-producing insects, which can complicate garden pest management. A trail in the kitchen is usually only the visible end of activity that extends outdoors.

proposedDescription: Argentine black and white tegu is a large, strong-bodied lizard with a banded tail. Young animals often have greenish heads. It eats a wide range of foods and can shelter in burrows during cold weather. Established populations in Florida are a concern because tegus eat native wildlife, including eggs and young animals; documented prey include alligator eggs and young gopher tortoises.
identification: Look for a large, sturdy black-and-white lizard with a long banded tail; young animals may have a green head.
actions: In Florida, photograph a suspected tegu, record the location, and report it to FWC. Never release a pet; use an approved surrender option instead.

sources.title: University of Florida IFAS: Florida Invader, Tegu Lizard
Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission: Argentine black and white tegu

researchNotes: FWC description, impacts and reporting passages and full UF Extension Florida Invader PDF read. Florida findings and reporting guidance are not generalized to all jurisdictions.
previousDescription: The Argentine black and white tegu is a large, ground-dwelling South American lizard with a banded or mottled body and a powerful tail. Young tegus often have green heads that fade as they grow. Adults eat a varied diet of fruit, insects, eggs, and small animals, and retreat into burrows during colder weather. In Florida, established populations raise conservation concerns because researchers have documented predation on native wildlife, including alligator eggs and young gopher tortoises. Its adaptable habits help explain why an escaped pet can become more than an isolated garden visitor.

proposedDescription: Argentine pepperweed is a hairy member of the mustard family with divided lower leaves and simpler leaves higher on the stem. Its small white flowers develop into flattened pods with a notch at the tip. The lower leaves may disappear as the plant matures, changing its overall appearance. Looking at both the remaining leaves and the seed pods helps distinguish it from other pepperweeds.
identification: Photograph lower and upper leaves, stem hairs, and ripe pods; compare with other Lepidium species.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Lepidium bonariense
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney: Lepidium bonariense

researchNotes: Full diagnostic descriptions from independent New Zealand and NSW floras read. Both support the changing leaf form and notched round fruit. Local impact and removal advice remain unsupported and are not asserted.
previousDescription: Argentine pepperweed is a small mustard relative whose seedpods are often easier to recognize than its tiny flowers. Lower leaves are deeply divided, while the leaves higher on a flowering stem become simpler. Hairy stems carry little pale flowers followed by flattened, rounded pods with a notch at the tip. Plants can look quite different as they mature and lose their lower leaves, so a complete photograph is more useful than a single flower. Records of naturalization describe where it grows outside its original range; they do not alone measure ecological damage.

proposedDescription: Aonidiella taxus is an armored scale found on yews, plum-yews and Podocarpus. A pale, partly transparent cover hides the reddish female beneath it, often on the underside of a leaf. Feeding can leave yellow patches around the insects. Its life also involves much smaller visitors: researchers in Japan found several kinds of tiny wasps parasitizing this scale. The cover and host plant offer useful clues, but related scales can look alike and a confident species identification requires microscopic examination.
identification: Inspect needle and leaf undersides for pale rounded scales and nearby yellowing; slide-mounted females are needed for confirmation.
actions: Avoid moving a suspect infested plant into a collection until its scales are identified.

sources.title: Uematsu1972: Studies on Marietta carnesi, I. Host Relation

researchNotes: Naturalis morphology/host/symptom passages read. Independent primary evidence is Uematsu1972 original abstract on parasitoids in Fukuoka/Miyazaki, read at journal host J-STAGE. Naturalis's Uematsu1978 life-history citation is a different work; do not count ScaleNet as an additional independent account. Earlier alternatives TARI2013 failed, Takagi1970 offered only brief host records, Stoetzel1975 abstract lacked biological detail. No efficacy recommendation inferred from parasitoid presence.
previousDescription: Aonidiella taxus is an armored scale found on plants such as yews, plum-yews and Podocarpus. A pale, partly translucent cover hides the reddish female beneath it. Feeding on leaf undersides can be associated with yellow patches. The young insects are mobile before settling down, and infested nursery plants can carry them to new locations even when the small scales are not immediately obvious.

supportedClaims: Pale translucent female cover, reddish adult, conifer hosts, leaf undersides, chlorosis, microscopic identification.
A.taxus parasitized by Comperiella, Aspidiotiphagus, Aphytis and Prospaltella in two Japanese localities.

proposedDescription: Arborvitae scale is a tiny armored insect associated with arborvitae, junipers and other conifers. Its cover can be oval or almost round, with a dull greenish-yellow color that becomes paler and browner with age. Infestations may accompany discolored foliage and dying twigs. A Pennsylvania study found a small parasitic wasp attacking this scale, and predatory mites sheltering in the empty scale covers afterward. Those observations reveal a small community around the insect, but do not establish a tested treatment for an infested tree.
identification: Look for pale yellowish armored scales on conifers; distinguish them from similar scales through expert examination.

sources.title: Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station, Bulletin 1059: armored scales
Schneider et al. 2019: arborvitae scale natural enemies (USDA ARS abstract)

researchNotes: Two independent biological evidence streams read: Connecticut Bulletin 1059 printed p138, drawing on Stimmel 2002 for phenology, and Schneider et al. 2019 primary Pennsylvania study abstract. ScaleNet morphology explicitly traces to Kuwana 1932; its repetition of 2019 is not counted independently. Connecticut phenology is regional and tentative and is omitted from profile. Parasitoid and mite observations do not support a control recommendation.
previousDescription: Dynaspidiotus pseudomeyeri is an armored scale associated with conifers, including arborvitae. Its raised, oval cover is yellowish when young and becomes browner with age. The insect feeds beneath this protective layer, which can make it look like a small bump on the plant. Natural enemies include tiny wasps and mites, although their presence does not guarantee that a particular infestation will remain harmless.

supportedClaims: Adult female cover is oval/irregular circular, convex, dull greenish yellow, aging pale yellow/brown.
Printed p138: conifer hosts; foliage discoloration and twig dieback; biology poorly known.
Encarsia perniciosi parasitized Pennsylvania scale; Cheletogenes ornatus mites nested in vacated scale cuticles.

proposedDescription: Gymnaspis aechmeae is a tiny armored scale sometimes called flyspeck scale. Its dark covering can resemble a speck of dirt on bromeliads and other ornamental plants, including those grown in greenhouses. The female remains within the skin from an earlier growth stage and produces live young that can crawl to new feeding sites. Infested plants provide a route for it to move between locations.
identification: Examine persistent dark specks on bromeliad leaves with magnification; confirm they are scales and have the species identified.
actions: Inspect new bromeliads before adding them to a collection and keep suspect plants apart while seeking identification and local advice.

sources.title: California Department of Food and Agriculture: Fly speck scale assessment

researchNotes: ScaleNet biological account and CDFA's independent 2013 greenhouse detection/risk assessment read. Historical California status is not presented as current; origin uncertainty retained.
previousDescription: Fly speck scale is aptly named: on a bromeliad, its small dark coverings can be mistaken for dirt. The insect has become a pest of bromeliad collections and greenhouse plants, where colonies can spoil the appearance of leaves. Mature females remain within a shed skin and produce mobile young rather than laying exposed eggs. Those crawlers can move between nearby plants, while the trade in living plants can carry the species much farther. Its native range is uncertain, so a precise origin story would overstate what the available evidence establishes.

proposedDescription: Mining scale can be easy to miss because plant tissue often partly hides its pale, rounded cover. The cover may be white, gray or yellow and is roughly three millimeters across at most. Howardia biclavis feeds on many kinds of woody plants. Researchers studying Mexican avocado orchards found it singly or in very small groups on branches, sometimes alongside other armored scales. Despite its common name, the exact way it becomes covered by plant tissue is not well understood, so it is better described as concealed than as a proven tunneling insect.
identification: Look for partly concealed rounded scale covers on bark; plant tissue can obscure their normal pale color.

sources.title: University of Hawaii CTAHR: Howardia biclavis
Lazaro-Castellanos et al. 2023: armored scales associated with Mexican avocados

researchNotes: Read CTAHR adult account and original 2023 study pp259–260. Independence is the Mexican authors' own branch-colony observations, not their ScaleNet/Watson background review. The paper explicitly questions whether crawlers can burrow and says biology remains little known; resolved by avoiding a tunneling assertion. Zenodo mirror repeatedly failed, replaced by accessible original journal PDF. CTAHR generic armored-scale generation duration is not treated as species-specific.
previousDescription: Howardia biclavis is an armored scale whose rounded, pale covering can become hidden by the host plant's outer tissue. This unusual feature has led to the name mining scale, although it is not a leaf-mining insect. It feeds on a range of woody plants. Because the covering blends into the plant surface, colonies may be less noticeable than exposed scales on leaves or stems.

supportedClaims: Pale rounded cover up to3mm often obscured by epidermis; broad host range.
pp259–260: Hass avocado branches, solitary or groups up to3, alongside other scales; burrowing mechanism uncertain.

proposedDescription: Lepidosaphes pinnaeformis leaves small brown, mussel-shaped covers on the leaves and sometimes stems of its hosts. Orchids are frequent hosts, and dense colonies can leave a patchwork of discolored feeding spots. The insect is not restricted to orchids: a Mexican orchard study also found it on avocado branches. Its covers can look much like those of other Lepidosaphes scales. A close view helps locate the insects, while microscopic features of the female are needed to distinguish similar species reliably.
identification: Check both sides of orchid leaves and stems for narrow brown shell-shaped covers and nearby discoloration.
actions: Inspect orchids before trading or introducing them into a collection; keep suspect plants separate for identification.

sources.title: Lazaro-Castellanos et al. 2023: armored scales associated with Mexican avocados

researchNotes: Naturalis full diagnostic, host, biology and symptom passages read; the independent 2023 paper pp260 reports original collections on avocado branches in small groups/individually, on Fuerte, Mexicano1 and Vitacalli. Its background citations to Watson/ScaleNet are not independent. Naturalis contains inconsistent older geographic statements (text says no Africa/Australia but later lists records); no absence/range assertion carried forward. 2024 Florida PDF inaccessible; original Mexican study supplies accessible independent evidence.
previousDescription: Lepidosaphes pinnaeformis is an armored scale associated with orchids. Its brown, elongated covering resembles a tiny mussel shell and may occur on leaves or stems. Feeding can discolor affected tissue. Newly hatched scales can crawl before settling, while established insects remain protected beneath their covers. Moving an infested orchid can transport the pest without the small colonies being noticed immediately.

supportedClaims: Brown mussel-like female covers2.4–3.5mm; orchids favored; leaf/stem feeding and discolored spots; slide mounting for identification.
p260: collected on avocado branches singly/small groups; similar covers to L.beckii.

proposedDescription: Fire bush scale often shelters between the corky ridges on winged euonymus twigs. Its female has a small brown, oyster-shaped cover with a pale body underneath. Lepidosaphes yanagicola also uses other deciduous trees and shrubs, including willow, maple and elm. Adult females can survive the winter and produce eggs the following summer. Heavy infestations sometimes accompany early leaf fall and twig dieback, although damage varies among locations. This is a different insect from Unaspis euonymi, another scale associated with euonymus.
identification: Inspect the grooves between winged euonymus bark ridges for narrow brown scales; do not equate every euonymus scale with Unaspis euonymi.

sources.title: University of Illinois Extension: Winged Euonymous Scale

researchNotes: Both complete biological accounts read. UMass includes Massachusetts crawler timing from Robert Childs and comparative Pennsylvania/Maryland damage; Illinois account by Schuster and Nixon supplies local southern-Illinois occurrence and life cycle. These are separate expert extension treatments with local observations, not a mirror. Conflict: Illinois says it does not move to leaves; UMass reports leaf midveins in heavy infestations. Profile says often on twigs and makes no absolute leaf-absence claim. Native origin omitted; no current treatment advice imported.
previousDescription: Lepidosaphes yanagicola is an armored scale with a brown, elongated cover. It occurs on woody plants, including the corky ridges of burning-bush stems, and has also been called firebush scale. Several scales use similar hosts, so the plant's name alone is not enough to identify it. In particular, it should not be confused with the different insect commonly called euonymus scale.

supportedClaims: Brown2mm female cover, white body, deciduous hosts, differs from U.euonymi, variable damage; adults overwinter.
Southern Illinois burning-bush twig-ridge colonies, June egg laying and adult overwintering, leaf drop/twig dieback.

proposedDescription: Harper scale can blend into bark even when several insects are present. Its narrow, nearly flat tan covers are only about one to two millimeters long, with darker shed skins at one end and a pink or red female underneath. It feeds on a variety of woody plants and often settles in bark cracks. A specialist comparing specimens from California, Japan and Taiwan confirmed how widely the same species had been recorded. Its sheltered position and resemblance to other scales make microscopic examination important for a reliable identification.
identification: Examine bark cracks in good light for narrow tan scales; reliable species identification requires microscopic examination.

sources.title: Takagi 1970: Diaspididae of Taiwan, Part II

researchNotes: Naturalis substantive account was read, with living appearance and bark habitat attributed to Gill1997. Takagi1970 pp29–31 is an independently examined morphological account: original Taiwan Hibiscus female plus direct comparison with California/Japan specimens. Its collection is stronger than a taxonomic listing. Naturalis references Takagi for geographic records; that repeated distribution alone is not counted twice. Historical California low damage and regulatory ratings are omitted rather than generalized or presented as current.
previousDescription: Neopinnaspis harperi is a small armored scale that can hide in bark crevices on woody plants. Its narrow, fairly flat cover is tan with a darker end, concealing a pinkish female underneath. The insect is only around one to two millimeters long. Available California accounts report limited known damage, and its small size and sheltered position make careful inspection more informative than a distant view of the plant.

supportedClaims: Tan flat1–2mm cover, red/pink female, bark cracks, broad woody hosts and difficult visual detection.
pp29–31: detailed female diagnosis, Hibiscus collection, direct California/Japan/Taiwan specimen comparison.

proposedDescription: Parlatoria camelliae is an armored scale found on camellias and other hosts. Its pale to gray covering has a darker patch made from earlier shed skins. Colonies can occur on either side of a leaf, often near veins, and feeding may discolor the foliage. Reports from places such as Galicia document its presence, but identification still requires attention to the insect rather than leaf discoloration alone.
identification: Inspect both leaf surfaces, especially near veins, and distinguish this species from tea scale and other camellia scales.

sources.title: International Camellia Society: Research on scale insects in Galicia

researchNotes: ScaleNet's exact biological notes and the primary Galicia survey hosted by International Camellia Society read. The survey documented leaf discoloration on two plants; it does not establish widespread severe harm or a general treatment need.
previousDescription: Camellia parlatoria scale settles on leaves as small pale to grayish covers with a darker patch of shed skin. It has been recorded from more hosts than its common name suggests. Observations on camellia found insects on both leaf surfaces, often near veins; researchers in Galicia also documented discoloration on affected plants. Such marks can prompt a closer look, but leaf discoloration has many causes and several scale species share camellias. The insect under the cover, rather than the plant's symptoms alone, is what allows a specialist to identify it.

proposedDescription: Rutherfordia major is an armored scale associated with lychee and other tropical woody plants. Its initially pale covering may become covered by plant tissue and appear reddish or dark, helping it blend into bark. It has been introduced to places including the Galapagos. Movement of host plants is relevant to its spread, while the full history of its original distribution remains less certain.
identification: Look for rounded to oval covers partly hidden by tissue, with brown shed skins near the edge; specialist confirmation is needed.
researchNotes: ScaleNet diagnostic and economic-importance passages and Charles Darwin Foundation's regional introduction and host record read. Galapagos invasive impact is explicitly listed as no data; old Florida pest concern is not represented as a current measured loss.
previousDescription: Lychee bark scale can be difficult to recognize because its normally white cover becomes obscured by plant tissue. The resulting patch may look reddish brown or almost black rather than snowy white. The insect uses a range of tropical woody hosts, not only lychee. Records from the Galapagos describe an established introduction associated with plant material, while older literature discusses possible importance on lychee in Florida. These are different kinds of evidence: an introduced population is not, by itself, proof of a measured ecological impact.

proposedDescription: Selenaspidus albus is an armored scale with a small white disk for a cover. Slightly off-center, yellow-brown remains of earlier growth stages form a contrasting patch. The female's cover is usually less than two millimeters across, making a single insect easy to overlook. Euphorbia is a documented host, and crowded colonies have been reported on cultivated plants. A British botanical-garden report also found a heavy infestation on an imported Euphorbia kept in a heated glasshouse.
identification: Examine white circular covers on Euphorbia with magnification; the off-center shed skins help detection but do not confirm the species.

sources.title: Malumphy et al.2010: First incursion of Contigaspis zillae, contextual S.albus record

researchNotes: ScaleNet's complete species account was read; its female-cover morphology is attributed to McKenzie (1953a), and its California dense-population note to Gill (1997). The independent Malumphy, Halstead & Salisbury (2010) original paper was read in full, using only the S. albus observation in the introductory paragraph on printed p219: Euphorbia caput-medusae imported from South Africa in 2007 was found heavily infested at Wisley in October 2009, where the plant had been kept in a heated glasshouse. This observation supplies a concrete host, infestation and living-plant transport context independent of the older morphology account. It is a short but substantive biological field note, sufficient for the narrowly scoped final paragraph; it does not establish uninterrupted infestation since import or general outdoor establishment, impact, life cycle or control. None of the paper's later Contigaspis zillae biology is transferred to S. albus. Attempts to obtain McKenzie's original through the CDFA index and the separate Malumphy & Halstead (2010), BJENH 23:45–50, yielded bibliography/metadata only and are not counted. Readiness rests on complementary claims in two independently authored biological accounts, not two duplicates of a complete life history.
previousDescription: Selenaspidus albus is an armored scale with a small, white, disk-shaped cover. A yellow-brown patch sits slightly off-center, marking the remains of earlier growth stages. It is associated with plants including Euphorbia. The covering is less than two millimeters across, so individual insects are easy to overlook; heavier colonies are more conspicuous and can warrant closer inspection of the host plant.

supportedClaims: Female cover about1.75mm, round white, subcentral yellow-brown exuviae; heavy Euphorbia populations recorded in California.

Printed p219 introductory paragraph, directly read: Euphorbia caput-medusae imported from South Africa in 2007 was found heavily infested by S. albus in October 2009 at Wisley; plants were kept in heated glasshouses.

This supports the description's documented Euphorbia host, heavy cultivated-plant infestation and living-plant transport context only. Later pages concern Contigaspis zillae and provide no S. albus evidence.

proposedDescription: West Indian red scale forms thin, partly transparent disks on leaves, often on the upper surface. Each female's cover has a pale edge and an off-center patch of darker shed skins. Citrus is a frequent host, but Selenaspidus articulatus feeds on many other plants, including rubber trees. Dense populations can cause yellowing and damaged leaf or fruit tissue. A field study in Brazil found that numbers on rubber trees changed with the season and differed among tree clones, so infestation levels should be assessed in their local setting.
identification: Inspect upper leaf surfaces for flat translucent scales with pale margins; use microscopic confirmation for a species record.
actions: Avoid transporting visibly infested plants and obtain a confirmed identification before selecting control.

sources.title: Silva etal2020: Population Fluctuation of Selenaspidus articulatus in Rubber Tree

researchNotes: Naturalis complete morphology, host, ecology and symptom sections read. Silva etal2020 original PDF methods/results pp1–4 directly read (public HTTP fallback after web reopen errors): fortnightly leaf sampling2013–2014, four rubber clones, Goianesia Brazil. Independent of older Naturalis synthesis. Seasonal peaks were specific to this study; no universal climate response, resistance guarantee or treatment threshold inferred.
previousDescription: Selenaspidus articulatus has a thin, partly transparent cover with a pale rim and an off-center darker patch. It feeds on citrus and many other plants, often on exposed upper leaf surfaces. Heavy infestations can cause yellowing and affect leaves or fruit. The name West Indian red scale appears in references, but a close look is needed to separate it from similar armored scales.

supportedClaims: Thin semitransparent round cover, pale rim, subcentral dark exuviae, upper leaf surfaces, citrus and other hosts; chlorosis and tissue injury.
Methods/results: leaf infestation in four Hevea clones varied seasonally and among clones during2013–2014.

proposedDescription: Unaspis citri is often noticed as a snowy white coating on citrus trunks and branches. That appearance comes largely from the white covers of immature males; females have darker, shell-shaped covers. Heavy feeding can weaken trees, contribute to branch dieback and cause bark to split. Its concentration on woody parts of the tree helps distinguish citrus snow scale from some scales found mainly on leaves.
identification: Look for clusters of white narrow male covers mixed with dark female covers on citrus trunks and limbs.
actions: Monitor trunks and major branches. Ask local citrus extension for identification and management guidance if live scales are abundant or bark injury is developing.

sources.title: University of Florida IFAS: Citrus Snow Scale
Clemson Extension: Citrus insects and related pests

researchNotes: UF IFAS life-stage and diagnostic passages and Clemson's species-specific damage section read. Clemson's wording about winged white males is not adopted: UF identifies the snowy covers as immature males. No treatment rate or calendar supplied.
previousDescription: Citrus snow scale can make a trunk or branch look as though it has been dusted white. The snowy appearance comes from the covers of immature males; females remain beneath darker, shell-shaped armor. Colonies are usually concentrated on citrus bark and larger limbs, with leaves and fruit involved when infestations are severe. Persistent heavy feeding can weaken a tree and contribute to branch dieback and splitting bark. Inspecting both the white male covers and the less noticeable females gives a much clearer picture than looking only for a white coating.

proposedDescription: This armored scale is listed as Andaspis punicae, though newer references also place it in Lepidosaphes. Its brown, elongated covering resembles a small shell on woody hosts, including lychee. Heavy populations may reduce plant vigor or damage branches. Changes in the scientific name can make records harder to connect, so both names are useful when checking the research behind an identification.
identification: Look for long, narrow dark covers on woody growth; have a specialist distinguish it from other lychee scales.

sources.title: USDA ARS: Andaspis punicae in lychee

researchNotes: ScaleNet morphology and current nomenclature plus the independent USDA-hosted 2006 primary study's complete interpretive summary and technical abstract read. The full proceedings paper was not read. Preserve the catalog ID; current combination is Lepidosaphes punicae. Association with corky bark is not stated as proven causation.
previousDescription: The scale historically called Andaspis punicae hides beneath a long, dark, mussel-shaped cover on woody plants. Current ScaleNet treatment places it in Lepidosaphes as Lepidosaphes punicae, so both names can appear in references to the same insect. Lychee is among its hosts, and research has linked infestations with loss of vigor and branch decline. The old name is worth retaining in a search, but a scale on lychee should still be identified carefully: several armored scales can share the crop and look like small pieces of bark.

proposedDescription: Snout scale is a tiny armored insect found on citrus and other plants. The female remains enclosed within a shed skin from an earlier stage, producing a brown, elongated covering with a conspicuous ridge along its back. Dense colonies may also leave white secretions on the leaves. The 'snout' is a much smaller feature of the female's head, visible with close microscopic study. Several related Fiorinia species look similar in the field, so the shape of a brown cover alone is not a reliable identification.
identification: Check leaf undersides for narrow ridged covers; specialist comparison with other Fiorinia is necessary.

Changed overly narrow glossy golden-brown cover wording to directly observed light-to-medium-dark brown. No broad damage/control inference.
previousDescription: Fiorinia proboscidaria is a small armored scale sometimes called snout scale. Its elongated covering is glossy and golden-brown, and the female remains protected within an earlier shed skin. It occurs on citrus and other plants. Several related scales look much alike, so the cover's general shape is only a starting point; reliable identification depends on more detailed examination.

pp180–186: ridged brown second-instar cover encloses female, white secretions on heavily infested leaves, conical head/process, citrus collections and comparative diagnosis.

proposedDescription: Aroma is a thorny shrub or small tree with finely divided leaves and hanging, two-tone flower heads. Pink or mauve sterile flowers contrast with the yellow fertile end, and clustered pods twist as they mature. Dichrostachys cinerea can establish from seed and spread through shoots arising from its roots, sometimes forming dense thickets. That growth occurs even within its native African range. A South African field study found root suckers among young plants under several fire and grazing regimes, showing why its spreading habit needs local context.
identification: Look for hanging two-tone flower heads, twice-divided leaves, sharp-tipped branches, and twisted pods.

previousDescription: Aroma is a thorny shrub or small tree with finely divided leaves and unusual hanging flowers: pink or mauve at one end and yellow at the other. Its pods become twisted as they mature. It can spread through both seed and shoots from its roots, producing dense thickets. Native across parts of the Old World, it has become invasive in some places outside that range.

Pink/purple sterile vs yellow fertile flower portions; twisted pods; prolific root suckers.

proposedDescription: Arrocillo is a coarse perennial grass that forms leafy clumps. Its broad blades may feel hairy or rough, while the flowering head opens into many slender, spreading branches. Tiny rounded spikelets sit in paired rows along those branches, a useful detail for identification. Paspalum paniculatum grows in disturbed clearings and other open ground. Its home range includes tropical America, while regional floras record it as introduced elsewhere, including the United States and Australia; a local record needs that regional context.
identification: Photograph a complete mature seed head and the arrangement of spikelets; leaf shape alone is insufficient.

Pohl and Davidse: Flora Mesoamericana, reproduced in WFO Paspalum paniculatum
