proposedDescription: Athel tamarisk is a large evergreen tree with fine, jointed-looking branches and tiny, scale-like leaves. Its deep roots and tolerance of dry, salty conditions have made it useful for shelter plantings. Outside cultivation, it can spread along waterways. In parts of Australia, dense stands have altered river habitats and soil conditions, showing how a tree valued for protection from wind can become a problem in the wrong setting.

sources.title: Oregon State University Landscape Plants: Tamarix aphylla

researchNotes: Read Oregon State's tree description and Queensland's biology/impacts page. Australian river-system effects are explicitly regional; a planting does not establish a U.S. invasive outcome.
previousDescription: Athel tamarisk is a large evergreen shrub or tree with a spreading crown and fine, jointed branchlets. Its tiny leaves hug the twigs, and clusters of pale pink to white flowers appear among the foliage. Deep roots and tolerance of drought and salty soils made it useful for shade and shelter in dry landscapes. It can also escape cultivation. In parts of Australia, dense riverbank infestations have altered water flow and soil salinity, illustrating why a hardy planted tree can become a management concern in some settings.

proposedDescription: Atlantic ivy is an evergreen vine that can carpet the ground or climb trees. Young growth has lobed leaves, while mature flowering growth has less-divided leaves and produces fruit eaten by birds. Stems can also root as they spread. Introduced populations in the Pacific Northwest can dominate forest ground cover and add weight to trees. It is closely related to, but distinct from, English ivy.

sources.title: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board: English and Irish ivy

researchNotes: Read Oregon State's ivy account and Washington's species/cultivar-specific findings page. The latter explicitly includes H. hibernica 'Hibernica'. Shared ivy traits are described without asserting that every cultivar has identical status.
previousDescription: Atlantic ivy, often called Irish ivy, is an evergreen climbing vine that can also make a thick carpet across the ground. Young shoots carry lobed leaves; flowering shoots have less-divided leaves and produce berries. Rooting stems expand a patch locally, while birds can carry seeds farther away. In invaded Pacific Northwest woodlands, dense ivy can cover native understory plants and add weight to trees. It closely resembles English ivy, and the species or cultivar should be confirmed when interpreting local weed guidance.

proposedDescription: Aucuba whitefly is a tiny sap-feeding insect that uses many host plants, including citrus and ivy. Its dark, oval immature stages sit on leaves and are easier to examine with magnification. Plants moved through trade can carry it between locations. A California assessment reported no significant known impacts at that time, so detection should be distinguished from evidence of serious damage.

sources.title: California Department of Food and Agriculture: Aleuroclava aucubae assessment
Seljak (2012): Six new alien phytophagous insects recorded in Slovenia

researchNotes: Read CDFA's 2022 assessment and Seljak's primary study, especially the A. aucubae section on pages 4-5. Identification relies on slide-mounted immature cases. Dated absence of reported damage is not proof of permanent harmlessness.
previousDescription: Aucuba whitefly is a tiny plant-feeding insect found on a wide range of trees and shrubs, including citrus, ivy, and ornamental evergreens. Its immature stages stay on leaves; the late immature cases are small, dark, and oval, and reliable identification requires magnification. Trade in infested plants can move it between regions. California's 2022 assessment reported no known significant economic or environmental damage there, while European observations likewise found limited injury. Finding the insect and demonstrating damage to its host are separate questions.

proposedDescription: Australasian geranium is a low-growing perennial with hairy, rounded leaves divided into lobes. Its small pink flowers have paler centers and usually appear singly or in pairs. Thickened roots support the plant in moist places such as gullies, creek margins and forested ground. The modest flowers and creeping or spreading growth can make it less conspicuous than familiar garden geraniums.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Geranium homeanum
Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria: Geranium homeanum

researchNotes: Read PlantNET and independently authored Flora of Victoria treatment. Both support a perennial, sprawling plant of moist habitats; no U.S. impact claim was added.
previousDescription: Australasian geranium is a low, sprawling perennial with coarse hairs and rounded leaves cut into several broad lobes. Small flowers, pink toward the tips and paler at the base, appear singly or in pairs. A thickened, branching root supports growth from season to season. In Australia it is associated with moist places such as creek banks, wet gullies, and forest margins. Its modest flowers and leaf shape help distinguish it from the more conspicuous plants commonly sold as garden geraniums.

proposedDescription: Australian backyard mosquito has white-banded legs, a pale ring on its mouthparts and lyre-shaped markings on its back. It breeds in small water collections, including tree holes and containers around homes. Adults may bite during the day in shaded places. Originally associated with Australasia, it has also been detected in California, where container habitats can provide suitable places for it to reproduce.

sources.title: Northern Territory Department of Health: Common mosquitoes, Aedes notoscriptus
Santa Barbara Mosquito and Vector Management District: Australian backyard mosquito

researchNotes: Read the NT Department of Health's species section and the Santa Barbara vector district's own detection/biology report. Kept diagnostic white proboscis band and container breeding; avoided inferring local human disease transmission.
previousDescription: Australian backyard mosquito is a dark mosquito with white-banded legs, pale lyre-shaped markings on its back, and a white ring around the middle of its long feeding tube. Its young use tree holes and rain-filled containers, including plant trays, buckets, and drains. Females bite people and other animals, sometimes during the day in shade. Recent detections in California show how this adaptable mosquito can become a neighborhood concern. Its markings matter because it closely resembles other introduced Aedes mosquitoes.

proposedDescription: Australian brake is a fern with large fronds divided into many narrow green segments. Brown stalks rise from a short base, and lines of spore-producing structures form along the undersides of the leaf edges. It grows naturally in Australasian forest and stream habitats and is also cultivated. Looking beneath a mature frond can reveal features that are less obvious from its overall shape.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Pteris tremula
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Pteris tremula

researchNotes: Read Flora of New Zealand and PlantNET botanical treatments. Natural habitat, frond form, and sori were compared. Cultivation or escape does not by itself establish invasive harm.
previousDescription: Australian brake is a large, lacy fern whose fronds divide repeatedly into narrow green segments. Brown stalks rise from a short, scaly base, and the fronds can move delicately in a breeze. Lines of spore-producing structures run near the underside edges of fertile segments. It grows in sheltered forest, streamside, and garden settings and has been cultivated beyond its Australasian range. Looking beneath a frond provides useful identification details that are easy to miss when seeing only its feathery outline.

proposedDescription: Australian cheesewood is an evergreen tree with glossy, wavy-edged leaves and fragrant white flowers. Orange capsules open to expose sticky seeds that birds can carry away. Native to eastern Australia, it has become weedy in some places outside its natural range. Its attractive foliage and scent explain its garden use, while bird-dispersed seeds help it move beyond planted sites.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria: Pittosporum undulatum

researchNotes: Read Stanford's observed tree account and Flora of Victoria's treatment. PIRSA returned navigation without substantive species text and was not used. Victoria's account explicitly distinguishes original native range from later expansion.
previousDescription: Australian cheesewood, or sweet pittosporum, is a shrub or tree with glossy leaves edged in gentle waves. Fragrant creamy-white flowers are followed by orange to yellow-brown capsules that open around sticky seeds. Birds help move those seeds away from planted trees. Although native to parts of eastern Australia, it has spread beyond its earlier range and become an environmental weed in some Australian forests and coastal scrub. Its familiar garden appearance can therefore mean different things depending on the local setting.

proposedDescription: Australian eelgrass is a freshwater plant with long, ribbon-like leaves rooted in the bottom. It spreads through runners and can form dense underwater beds. Female flowers reach the surface, and their stalks coil after pollination. Despite the common name, it is not a marine seagrass. Introduced populations occur in places including California's Delta, where its underwater growth can change the structure of aquatic habitat.

sources.title: California Department of Parks and Recreation: Ribbon weed identification
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Vallisneria australis

researchNotes: Read California's ribbon-weed identification sheet and PlantNET's species treatment. Distinguished freshwater Vallisneria from marine eelgrass and avoided transferring other Vallisneria species' impacts.
previousDescription: Australian eelgrass, also called ribbon weed, is a freshwater plant with long, strap-shaped leaves rising from the sediment. Underground runners connect neighboring plants into tall underwater meadows. Small female flowers reach the surface on slender stalks, which coil back underwater after pollination. Despite the name eelgrass, it is not a marine seagrass. Introduced populations have been documented in California's Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, where distinguishing it from other ribbonlike aquatic plants helps track changes in submerged vegetation.

proposedDescription: Australian fingergrass is easiest to recognize by its little windmill-shaped seed heads. Usually six to nine slender branches spread almost horizontally from the top of a stem, with the florets turning dark as they mature. Narrow leaves form a low, dense clump beneath flowering stems that can reach about knee height. Native to Australia, it grows on varied soils and flowers in response to rain. The detached seed heads can tumble in the wind, helping scatter seed.

sources.title: PlantNET NSW Flora Online: Chloris truncata
NSW Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development: Windmill grass

researchNotes: Read the complete PlantNET treatment by Jacobs and Hastings and the independently written NSW DPIRD Grassed Up agronomy account. These provide separate detailed botanical and growth/dispersal observations despite both being NSW institutions. Corrected the earlier wording: mature florets/spikelets darken, not necessarily the supporting branches. Accounts call it perennial versus biennial/short-lived perennial; avoided an unnecessarily rigid lifespan. No US impact or weed-status claim is inferred.
previousDescription: Australian fingergrass has a seed head shaped like a small windmill, with narrow branches spreading outward in a roughly horizontal plane. It forms low clumps with narrow leaves, and the flowering branches darken as they mature. Native to Australia, it responds to rainfall and grows on a range of soils. The spoke-like head is its clearest feature when seen among other grasses.

supportedClaims: Dense low crown, narrow leaves and flowering stems to 0.5 m.
Usually 6–9 horizontally radiating spikes; black mature florets.
Rain-responsive flowering and occurrence on varied soils.
Australian native warm-season grass, dense crown and windmill heads.
Rain-responsive growth on several soil types.
Mature detached heads can roll and disperse seed.

proposedDescription: Australian lovegrass is a loosely tufted perennial with narrow leaves and open, branching flower heads. Small, layered flower clusters sit along the fine branches, and hairs near the leaf joints can help with identification. It is native to eastern and southeastern Australia, where it grows in woodland and pasture settings. It should not be confused with other lovegrasses that have different ranges and impacts.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew GrassBase: Eragrostis leptostachya
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Eragrostis leptostachya

researchNotes: Read Kew GrassBase and PlantNET botanical descriptions. Used broad, concordant morphology rather than incompatible exact floret-count ranges. Did not transfer the reputation of other Eragrostis species to this one.
previousDescription: Australian lovegrass, also known as paddock lovegrass, is a slender perennial that grows in loose tufts. Narrow leaves sit below an open, branching flower head made of many small, neatly stacked spikelets. A tiny fringe of hairs where the leaf meets the stem provides another identification clue. Native to eastern and southeastern Australia, it occurs in woodland and native pasture. Several unrelated concerns are attached to other plants called lovegrass, so the scientific name matters when deciding what a local observation means.

proposedDescription: Australian redcedar can become a very large rainforest tree, with leaves divided into pointed leaflets and new growth often tinged red or pink. Older trees develop rough bark and may have broad buttresses at the base. Woody fruits release winged seeds. Its valuable timber led to extensive historical logging, and trees growing in open sites can look quite different from tall forest-grown specimens.

sources.title: Australian National Botanic Gardens: Toona ciliata
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Toona ciliata

researchNotes: Read ANBG's horticultural account and PlantNET's botanical treatment. The earlier draft's Botanic Gardens palms URL is unrelated and has been excluded. No U.S. invasive designation inferred from seed production.
previousDescription: Australian redcedar is a large deciduous rainforest tree with long leaves divided into many pointed leaflets. New foliage can flush reddish pink, while mature trunks develop scaly bark and substantial buttress roots. Small pale flowers are followed by woody capsules that release winged seeds. Its rich-colored, workable timber made it historically valuable and led to extensive logging in Australia. The shape also changes with its surroundings: forest trees can grow tall and straight, while open-grown trees develop broader spreading crowns.

proposedDescription: Australian redclaw crayfish is a large freshwater crayfish, often blue-green, with a distinctive red patch on the claws of mature males. It comes from northern Australia and nearby regions, using streams, lakes and seasonally changing waters. Widely farmed for food, it can escape cultivation. It eats a variety of plant and animal material, making its establishment relevant to the waters and species it encounters.

sources.title: Joyce and Pirozzi: Stable-isotope study of farmed redclaw diet
Australian Government: Freshwater Pest Field Guide, redclaw

researchNotes: Read Queensland's aquaculture guidance, the James Cook University primary feeding study, and the 2025 Northern Australia field guide's redclaw section. The field guide supports male claw markings and regional pest context; feeding-trial findings are not presented as a wild impact experiment.
previousDescription: Australian redclaw crayfish is a large freshwater crayfish, usually mottled blue-green. Mature males have a soft, bright red patch along the outer edge of each large claw, a useful identification clue. It uses tropical streams, lakes, and billabongs in its native northern Australian range and is also farmed for food. It eats a varied diet that includes naturally occurring pond organisms and plant material. Movement for aquaculture has taken it beyond its home waters, where escaped populations can interact with local species.

proposedDescription: Australian saltbush is a low, spreading plant that can form a mat over dry or salty ground. Its gray-green leaves have a fine coating, especially beneath, and its seed-bearing structures become fleshy and red. It has been planted for forage and erosion control. Animals can spread its seeds, and it has established outside cultivation in places including coastal California.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew: Atriplex semibaccata, Flora of Iraq and Flora of Tropical East Africa
California Invasive Plant Council: Australian saltbush

researchNotes: Read Kew-hosted botanical descriptions and Cal-IPC's detailed plant report. Combined morphology, historical planting, dispersal, and California habitat context without suggesting identical impacts nationwide.
previousDescription: Australian saltbush is a low, spreading perennial that can form broad mats above a deep woody root. Small gray-green leaves often look dusted underneath, and the seed is enclosed in fleshy reddish structures. Native to Australia, it was introduced elsewhere for uses including forage and erosion control. It tolerates dry and salty ground and has colonized disturbed coastal habitats in California. Animals can carry its seeds, helping explain how a plant close to the ground can establish new patches some distance away.

proposedDescription: Australian teatree is a shrub or small tree with gray-green leaves, white flowers and persistent woody seed capsules. Older plants may have twisted trunks and textured bark. Native to coastal southeastern Australia, it has been planted as a screen and windbreak and has become invasive in some other regions. Newer botanical references may list it as Gaudium laevigatum rather than Leptospermum laevigatum.

sources.title: Australian National Botanic Gardens: Leptospermum laevigatum

researchNotes: Read Stanford's observed-tree description and ANBG's species account. Recent Gaudium usage is framed as a name encountered in newer treatments, not an editorial taxonomy replacement.
previousDescription: Australian teatree is a shrub or small tree with gray-green leaves, white flowers, and flat-topped woody seed capsules. Older plants can develop wonderfully twisted trunks and shaggy bark. Native to coastal southeastern Australia, it tolerates salt spray and has been planted as a screen or windbreak. It has also naturalized beyond its original range and become weedy in some regions. Recent botanical treatments may use Gaudium laevigatum, so both names are helpful when matching observations with planting records or identification guides.

proposedDescription: Australian tortoise beetle is a rounded brown beetle, often mottled with darker marks, that feeds on eucalyptus. Adults and larvae chew the leaves, leaving curved or semicircular notches along the edges. Adults commonly feed at night and shelter beneath loose bark during the day, a habit also documented in Chilean field collections. Introduced populations occur in California. Established, well-cared-for trees often tolerate feeding, although heavy defoliation can add stress; finding beetles does not by itself show how seriously a tree is affected.

sources.title: UC Integrated Pest Management: Eucalyptus tortoise beetles
Villablanca and Villablanca Miranda (2022): Trachymela sloanei field record in Chile

researchNotes: Read UC IPM's complete combined tortoise-beetle account, distinguishing Trachymela sloanei from the other beetle covered, and Villablanca/Villablanca Miranda's original Chilean field report (2022). The latter independently documents specimens associated with Eucalyptus camaldulensis and shelter beneath bark. California damage severity and tree tolerance are supported by UC, not extrapolated from the Chilean collection. Retained that established trees often tolerate feeding, not a guarantee of harmlessness.
previousDescription: Australian tortoise beetle is a rounded brown beetle associated with eucalyptus. Adults and larvae feed on leaves, often leaving curved or semicircular notches along the edges. Adults commonly feed at night and shelter beneath bark during the day. Introduced populations occur in California. Mature trees can often tolerate some feeding, so the presence of beetles and the severity of damage should be assessed separately.

Night feeding, daytime bark shelter and curved edge notches.
California introduction and frequent tolerance of feeding by established well-maintained trees.

Independent eucalyptus association and bark-sheltering observation.
Australian origin and Chilean record; no California impact extrapolation.

proposedDescription: Australian tubeworm lives inside a hard, pale tube attached to a submerged surface. A feathery crown reaches into the water to collect tiny food particles, then withdraws into the tube when disturbed. It favors sheltered brackish places such as estuaries, lagoons and docks. Many generations can build tangled, reef-like colonies, although reefs do not form everywhere it occurs. It also grows on boat hulls and structures. Despite its common name, an Australian native origin remains uncertain.

sources.title: Richards (2008), Marine Biological Association MarLIN: A fanworm

researchNotes: Read Smithsonian's complete morphology/ecology sections and Richards's independently authored Marine Biological Association MarLIN review, including its diagnostic morphology, habitat and feeding details. Shared classic references exist, but MarLIN is a separate substantive synthesis with additional regional/biological literature, not the California mirror of Smithsonian. The failed MDPI paper is not counted as read. Both accounts treat Australian origin as possible, not established. Reef development is explicitly conditional; no reef is assumed at every occurrence.
previousDescription: Australian tubeworm builds hard, pale tubes in brackish water. A feathery crown extends from each tube to collect food, while large colonies can form reef-like structures on submerged surfaces. It also grows on boats and marine infrastructure, which can help it travel. Despite its common name, its original native range is uncertain; the name should not be treated as proof of an Australian origin.

supportedClaims: Pale calcareous tube, retractile radioles and feeding on suspended plankton.
Brackish estuarine habitat and attachment to hard submerged surfaces.
Conditional multi-generation reef formation and uncertain original range.
White calcareous tubes, paired featherlike feeding structures and suspension feeding.
Warm shallow/brackish estuaries, docks and lagoons; hulls and pipes as substrates.
Large colonies possible; Australia described only as a possible origin.

proposedDescription: Australian waterbuttons is a small, low-growing plant with finely divided leaves and tiny flower heads that look like buttons. The heads are cream to pale yellow and lack the showy outer petals of many daisies. Slender stems may lie along the ground or turn upward, and can root where they touch suitable soil. Look for it in lawns, roadsides, open grassland and other disturbed places. Its modest size can make the button heads easier to notice than the plant beneath them.

sources.title: PlantNET NSW Flora Online: Cotula australis
Kew-hosted Flora of Tropical East Africa (2005): Cotula australis

researchNotes: Read PlantNET's full description and the independently authored Flora of Tropical East Africa treatment (2005), hosted by Kew. Both provide substantive habit, divided-leaf and flower-head morphology, with wet/disturbed habitat information. This replaces the earlier insufficient NZPCN corroboration. Sources vary in annual/perennial wording and modern native-range delimitation; neither was needed for this identification-focused profile. Omitted a restrictive Australia/New Zealand-only origin and did not infer US ecological impact from lawn occurrence.
previousDescription: Australian waterbuttons is a small plant with finely divided leaves and tiny, cream to yellow flower heads that resemble buttons. The heads lack the showy outer petals of many familiar daisies. Stems can root where they touch suitable ground. Native to Australia and New Zealand, it also occurs in lawns, roadsides and other disturbed places elsewhere, often remaining close to the soil surface.

supportedClaims: Low prostrate/ascending habit and occasional rooting at nodes.
Finely divided leaves and small cream/pale-yellow heads with no showy outer corollas.
Roadside, lawn and open-grassland habitat.
Small prostrate or ascending herb with divided leaves.
Outer florets without corolla; inner florets pale white/yellow-green.
Moist garden and disturbed-ground habitat.

proposedDescription: Austrian pine has stiff, dark green needles held in pairs. Young trees are often roughly pyramid-shaped, while older trees develop broader crowns, deeply furrowed bark and brown cones. Native across parts of Europe, northwestern Africa and western Asia, it has been widely planted for screens and windbreaks. Its paired needles and mature bark are useful features when comparing it with other planted pines.

proposedDescription: Bean common mosaic necrosis virus is a plant virus that affects beans and related legumes. In some varieties, infection triggers darkening veins, wilt and widespread tissue death; in others it resembles ordinary bean common mosaic. Infected seed can introduce the virus, and aphids spread it between plants during brief feeding visits. Because related viruses can cause similar symptoms, laboratory testing is needed to distinguish them reliably.

proposedDescription: Bean weevil is a small seed beetle that develops inside dry beans. Adults have mottled brown, black and gray wing covers and lack the long snout associated with true weevils. The larvae chew within seeds, often remaining hidden until an adult leaves a neat round exit hole. Infestations can begin in the field and continue through repeated generations in warm storage. Moving infested seed has carried the beetle widely, and apparently intact beans can already contain developing larvae.
identification: Small mottled beetles without a long snout; round holes in stored beans and pale larvae within seeds.
actions: Inspect stored beans, isolate affected lots and keep clean seed in sealed containers; seek storage-pest advice for valued planting seed.
researchNotes: Seed beetle in Chrysomelidae, not a true snout weevil. Rutgers timing and host breadth are not generalized beyond beans; no unverified eradication recipe included.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Fisher and Carll Rutgers extension synthesis
claims: Mottled adults, hidden larval feeding, exit holes and storage development
Bean weevil identification and stored-seed damage

proposedDescription: Bear’s breeches is a clump-forming perennial with large, glossy leaves cut into deep lobes. Tall flower spikes rise above the foliage, carrying white flowers surrounded by purple-toned, spiny structures. The leaf shape is familiar from classical architectural decoration. Native around parts of the Mediterranean, it is grown widely as an ornamental in sun or partial shade. Underground stems allow an established clump to spread, and pieces left in the soil can make it difficult to remove completely.
identification: Large glossy, deeply lobed basal leaves and tall spikes of white flowers with purple, spiny bracts.
actions: Place cultivated plants where their spread can be contained; remove unwanted root pieces and check for regrowth.
researchNotes: NCSU generalized invasive wording omitted without a named affected region; description distinguishes vigorous garden spread from national invasive status.

claims: Leaves, flower spikes, classical motif and rhizome spread
Mediterranean native range and perennial habit

proposedDescription: Beardless rabbitsfoot grass is a moisture-loving grass that forms loose tufts and can spread through creeping stems that root where they touch the ground. Its narrow, flat leaves rise beneath dense, branched flower heads, usually green and sometimes tinged purple. Unlike the conspicuously bristly heads of some related grasses, its tiny flower clusters lack long awns. It grows beside ditches and waterways and on other damp ground, with a native range spanning parts of southern Europe, Africa and Asia.
identification: Look for creeping, rooting stems and compact, lobed green flower heads without long projecting bristles; a grass key is needed for similar species.
actions: Photograph the whole plant, flower head and rooting stems. Confirm its identity and local status before removing wetland vegetation.
researchNotes: Regional habitat and morphology are supported independently by Haines/Go Botany and Edgar and Connor's New Zealand flora; New Zealand descriptions allow annual or perennial plants. No nationwide invasive designation inferred.

proposedDescription: Bed bugs are small, blood-feeding insects that hide in narrow spaces close to where people rest. Unfed adults are flat, oval and brown, roughly the size of an apple seed; after feeding they become fuller and redder. Young bugs are smaller and much paler. They shelter in mattress seams, bed frames, furniture and other cracks, and can travel with luggage or belongings. Finding the insect itself, shed skins or dark spotting is more useful for identification than a pattern of skin bites.
identification: Adults are flat, brown and oval; young stages are pale. Inspect seams and crevices for bugs, shed skins and dark marks, and have suspected specimens identified.
actions: Keep suspected items contained rather than moving them between rooms. Seek identification and an integrated treatment plan from a qualified pest professional.
researchNotes: EPA morphology and University of Minnesota household entomology guidance are separate institutional accounts. Bite appearance does not establish a bed bug diagnosis; no disease-transmission or medical-treatment claim is needed.

claims: Adult and nymph appearance; identification before treatment.
Hiding sites; transport on belongings; signs; professional integrated management.

proposedDescription: Beech aphids are tiny sap-feeding insects most easily noticed through the white, woolly wax that gathers beneath beech leaves. The insects underneath are pale yellow, and their feeding can curl leaves downward. Sticky honeydew may fall onto lower foliage and support dark sooty mold. On European beech, eggs spend winter in bark crevices before colonies develop on new leaves. Infestations can spoil the appearance of leaves, although established, healthy trees often tolerate them without lasting harm.
identification: Check leaf undersides for pale aphids wrapped in white wax, sticky deposits and downward-curled leaf edges. Wool on bark alone points to other possible insects.
actions: Monitor tree condition and encourage natural enemies. Healthy established beeches often need no intervention; obtain an identification before treating persistent damage.
researchNotes: RHS practical account is independent of Kot and Kmiec's 2012 field study on Fagus sylvatica and cultivars. Do not confuse Phyllaphis fagi with the American beech blight aphid or beech scale.

claims: Pale aphids, wax, honeydew and sooty mold; usually tolerated by healthy trees.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Kot and Kmiec 2012 original field study
claims: European beech hosts; overwintering eggs in bark crevices; leaf curling.

proposedDescription: Neonectria coccinea is a fungus associated with bark disease in European beech. It can live in beech tissues without obvious symptoms, but it has also been recovered from declining trees and shown experimentally to cause substantial bark lesions. These injured patches can be part of more complicated tree decline involving stress and other fungi. The species is closely related to fungi involved in North American beech bark disease, so an affected tree's appearance alone cannot establish which fungus is present.
identification: Bark lesions or dieback warrant examination, but symptoms are not species-specific. Reliable identification requires laboratory work, including microscopic or DNA comparisons.
actions: Have unexplained beech bark damage assessed by a tree-health specialist. Record the host and location, and avoid assigning a fungal name from symptoms alone.
researchNotes: Important catalog distinction: modern N. coccinea is separated from North American N. faginata, historically called N. coccinea var. faginata. Castlebury et al. 2006 studied taxonomy; Langer and Busskamp 2021 independently tested European isolates. No US occurrence or introduced status inferred.

proposedDescription: Neonectria faginata is one of the fungi involved in beech bark disease in North America. The disease develops through an interaction between beech scale insects and fungi: scale feeding damages the bark, creating entry points for infection. Affected American beeches develop sunken or swollen areas of dead bark that may merge into larger cankers. The white, woolly material often seen earlier on the trunk belongs to the scale insects. Fungal identification requires closer examination than the tree's outward symptoms.
identification: Look for beech scale's white wax followed by patches of damaged, cankered bark. A plant laboratory must distinguish N. faginata from other canker fungi.
actions: Ask a tree-health professional to assess affected trees and any structural risk. Photograph bark symptoms and retain the location and host identity for diagnosis.
researchNotes: Retain separate catalog ID from N. coccinea. Castlebury et al. 2006 elevated the former N. coccinea var. faginata. NRCan's heading correctly uses N. faginata but its body retains obsolete Nectria coccinea terminology; used for the Canadian disease complex, reconciled against the original taxonomy. Do not equate the fungus with the entire disease or declare it introduced.

proposedDescription: Beech leaf disease is associated with a microscopic leaf nematode, Litylenchus crenatae subsp. mccannii. A distinctive early sign is dark banding between the veins of beech leaves, especially when viewed against the light. More affected leaves may become thick, curled or misshapen, while damaged buds produce fewer leaves and the crown gradually thins. The nematodes spend winter in buds and affect developing foliage. American, European and Oriental beeches can develop the disease, so host species alone does not rule it out.
identification: Hold a leaf toward the light to check for dark interveinal bands, and compare nearby leaves for thickening and distortion. Confirmation needs specialist assessment.
actions: Photograph several leaves and the whole tree, and contact local Extension or a plant diagnostic laboratory. Avoid transporting affected beech material to new sites.
researchNotes: Duplicate taxon context: this disease-oriented ID and litylenchus-crenatae-ssp-mccannii refer to the same named nematode subspecies; preserve both IDs pending editorial taxonomy review. Carta et al. 2020 original description and inoculation study is the underlying cause evidence; UMD supplies independent regional observations and practical recognition, while citing that research for causality.

proposedDescription: The beech tree nematode is a microscopic roundworm associated with beech leaf disease. It lives in developing buds and leaves, where its presence is linked to dark bands between leaf veins and to thickened, distorted foliage. Heavy damage can prevent buds from opening normally and leave the crown sparse. Researchers distinguished this North American subspecies from the previously described Japanese Litylenchus crenatae using body features and DNA, and reproduced disease symptoms by introducing nematodes into beech buds.
identification: The nematode itself is too small for ordinary field identification. Dark bands between leaf veins are a useful warning sign, but laboratory examination confirms the organism.
actions: Seek a plant diagnostic service for suspicious beech leaves. Keep the tree's location and photographs with the report and avoid moving affected planting material.
researchNotes: Same biological taxon as catalog beech-leaf-disease; retain both stable IDs, do not count them as two distinct nematodes. Supported form is Litylenchus crenatae subsp. mccannii; the paper title sometimes omits the rank. UMD draws causality from Carta et al.; its regional symptom observations are independently authored. No origin or universal invasive-status claim made.

proposedDescription: Beefsteakplant is an aromatic annual in the mint family, native to Asia and introduced in many parts of North America. It has opposite, toothed leaves on square stems, with small flowers grouped along upright spikes. Common ornamental forms have broad, crinkled, purple to reddish leaves. Plants produce abundant seed and may appear beyond gardens along roadsides or in other disturbed ground. Despite its history of cultivation, it can be troublesome in pastures because the plant is toxic to livestock.
identification: Check for opposite, broad toothed leaves, square stems and small flowers in narrow spikes. Leaf color varies among forms and is not enough for identification.
actions: Keep suspected plants out of livestock forage and seek local Extension advice on pasture infestations. Where removal is appropriate, act before seed develops.
researchNotes: Species includes multiple varieties and cultivated forms; purple foliage is not universal. NC State provides independently authored horticultural and regional weed information; Kew/WCVP supports accepted name and range. No edible-use recommendation or nationwide invasive designation.

proposedDescription: Beet armyworm is a moth whose caterpillars feed on many vegetables, field crops and weeds. Young larvae gather together and scrape leaf surfaces, sometimes leaving thin, windowlike patches and loose webbing. Older caterpillars spread out, chew irregular holes and may enter developing fruit. They are usually green with lengthwise stripes and a small dark spot near the second pair of true legs. Adults are mottled gray-brown moths, while eggs occur in clusters beneath a covering of pale, hairlike scales.
identification: Look for smooth, striped caterpillars with a dark spot above the second true leg, scale-covered egg clusters and grouped young larvae. Similar armyworms require closer comparison.
actions: Inspect leaves and developing fruit regularly and preserve beneficial insects where possible. Have damaging caterpillars identified before choosing crop-specific controls.
researchNotes: Independent UF entomology gallery and UC crop IPM account agree on larval characters and feeding. Generation counts and seasonal activity vary with climate, so regional California timing is omitted.

claims: Moth and caterpillar appearance; crop host groups.

proposedDescription: Bell's honeysuckle is a dense, many-stemmed shrub produced by crosses between Morrow's and Tatarian honeysuckles. It bears opposite, oval leaves and paired tubular flowers, often pink when fresh and yellow as they age. Red or orange berries follow and can be carried by birds. The hybrid is variable, with leaves and twigs ranging from nearly hairless to lightly downy. In parts of the northeastern and midwestern United States it grows along woodland edges, roadsides and old fields, sometimes forming dense stands.
identification: Look for paired flowers and berries, opposite smooth-edged leaves and older stems with hollow centers. Hybrid identification needs comparison with both parent species.
actions: Where locally invasive, remove small plants with their roots before fruiting and check for regrowth. Confirm identity first, especially near native honeysuckles.
researchNotes: Hybrid formula L. morrowii × L. tatarica; preserve the x-bella ID. Go Botany evidence is specifically the hybrid paragraph in the Morrow's honeysuckle account, not its main species description. Wisconsin DNR cites Czarapata and regional weed sources; Haines supplies independently authored hybrid diagnosis. Regional behavior is not a national designation.

proposedDescription: Polygonum patulum is a slender annual knotweed with upright stems that branch near the base. Narrow, pointed leaves are larger low on the plant and become much smaller toward the flowering branches. Tiny greenish or pink flowers gather around the stem joints, with many crowded near branch tips. Thin, papery sheaths surround the joints below the leaves. Native across parts of Europe and Asia, it occurs in fields, gardens and other open ground, including seasonally flooded places.
identification: Check the upright branching habit, narrow leaves, papery joint sheaths and tiny flowers near branch tips. Mature fruit and a regional key are needed for similar knotweeds.
actions: Photograph stem joints, leaves, flowers and mature fruit for a botanist. Establish local status and identity before deciding whether control is appropriate.
researchNotes: Catalog common name Bellard's smartweed is potentially confusing: P. bellardii has been misapplied to P. patulum, while some floras separate them. Description follows P. patulum M.Bieb. in Kew-hosted Flora of Iraq; China's independently authored key supports annual erect habit and reduced upper leaves. Fruit texture and leaf persistence differ among accounts, so omitted. No US presence or invasion inferred.

proposedDescription: Bellyache bush is a branching tropical shrub with leaves divided into three to five pointed lobes. Leaf stalks and margins carry sticky, gland-tipped hairs, and the foliage may be green or reddish purple. Small red to purple flowers develop in clusters, followed by rounded seed capsules. Native from Mexico through tropical America, it has escaped cultivation elsewhere. In northern Australia it forms dense stands around waterways and disturbed land. Its toxicity makes it a concern where people or livestock might consume it.
identification: Look for lobed leaves with sticky hairs on their stalks and edges, small reddish flowers and seed capsules. Green-leaved plants occur as well as purple forms.
actions: Keep the plant and seed away from livestock and children. Seek local weed advice; avoid spreading seed or stem and root pieces during removal.
researchNotes: Independent Proctor Flora of the Cayman Islands account, hosted by Kew, corroborates morphology and open-ground habitat; Northern Territory guidance supplies region-specific spread and toxicity. Avoid copying NT page's stray gamba heading and do not generalize Australian legal status.

proposedDescription: Belted spider beetles are small beetles that sometimes occur in stored products and buildings. Adults are roughly two to four millimeters long, with patches of pale scales near the front and rear of their wing covers. Males are more parallel-sided, while females look rounder. The species is native to Europe and North Africa and has been introduced to North America. Canadian records include warehouses and homes, and an early United States report documented it breeding in bags of stored flour.
identification: Use magnification to examine the pale patches on the wing covers and the evenly distributed hairs on the shield behind the head. Similar spider beetles need specialist comparison.
actions: If beetles appear in stored food, isolate the suspect package and inspect nearby dry goods. Have specimens identified before deciding how to address the source.
researchNotes: Bousquet's Canadian identification guide provides specimen-based morphology and occurrence. Cotton and Good's USDA publication independently cites Bureau records for flour breeding in Nebraska (entry 145, printed page 26); this is historical evidence, not a current abundance estimate. Japan/feed-mill text near the Canadian entry belongs to a different beetle and was excluded.

proposedDescription: Bengal trumpet is a long-lived climbing vine with large, pale blue to violet flowers and pale throats. Its opposite leaves are variable, often bearing broad teeth or shallow pointed lobes, and young stems are square in cross-section. Thickened underground roots help the plant persist. Native to southern Asia and grown for its flowers, it can become an environmental weed in warm regions such as Queensland. The blossoms attract bees, including large carpenter bees, and flowers may be followed by distinctly beaked capsules.
identification: Look for trumpet-shaped blue or violet flowers, opposite toothed or lobed leaves and paired leafy bracts beneath each flower. Compare with related cultivated Thunbergia vines.
actions: Check local weed status before planting or sharing it. For escaped vines, obtain a plan that addresses the persistent roots and keeps cut material out of natural areas.
researchNotes: Brisbane's species account supplies morphology and Queensland impact; Singapore NParks independently supplies horticultural and bee-visitor observations. The NSW page timed out and was not counted. Avoid conflating T. grandiflora with T. laurifolia solely from a shared clock-vine common name.

claims: Tuberous roots; opposite toothed leaves; trumpet flowers; Queensland environmental weed.
Climbing ornamental; Indian native occurrence; carpenter and blue-banded bee visitors.

proposedDescription: Bent-grass nematode is a microscopic roundworm that develops inside abnormal growths in grass flower heads. These elongated galls replace developing seeds and can be concealed by the surrounding flower parts. Bentgrasses are the best-known hosts, and a modern study also confirmed the species in fowl bluegrass beside a Wyoming river. Older accounts assigned many other grasses to this nematode, but some of those records belong to different species. Accurate identification therefore depends on examining the nematodes, not just noticing damaged seed heads.
identification: Unusually elongated flower parts and seed-replacing galls are useful warning signs. Microscopic and, where needed, DNA examination are necessary for species identification.
actions: Do not distribute suspect grass seed lots. Ask a seed-testing or plant diagnostic laboratory to examine galls and advise on cleaning or disposal.
researchNotes: Strong taxonomy caveat: older A. agrostis sensu lato host and bacterial-toxicity accounts cannot be transferred indiscriminately. Roubtsova/Subbotin 2020 molecularly confirmed Poa palustris; Eisenback/Roane 2006 is an independent morphology-based grass-gall study, but its A. stolonifera host record predates the narrow modern synthesis. Nemaplex repeats both lineages and is not a third independent experiment. No chemical, hot-water or burning prescription.

proposedDescription: Agrostis castellana is a perennial bentgrass with fine, gray-green leaves and upright flowering stems. It forms tufts linked by slender underground stems, while its flower head spreads into a delicate branching shape and often narrows as it ages. The tiny flower clusters may be greenish or purple, with some bearing slender awns and others lacking them. Native around the Mediterranean and nearby Atlantic islands, it has been introduced elsewhere, including New Zealand, where it is known as dryland browntop.
identification: Look for fine gray-green leaves, underground spreading stems and an open flower head with a mixture of awned and awnless flower clusters. A grass key is needed.
actions: Have flowering material identified before managing an unfamiliar patch. Check local guidance and avoid moving seed or soil from unwanted stands.
researchNotes: Catalog Bentgrass is nonspecific; dryland browntop is supported by Edgar and Connor. Independent New Zealand flora and Kew/WCVP support morphology and range. No US invasive status inferred and no traits copied from unrelated Agrostis entries or old synonym descriptions.

proposedDescription: Lachnagrostis filiformis is a fine-leaved grass native to Australia, often growing on poorly drained or seasonally wet ground. Its loose, airy flower head branches widely above a tuft of narrow leaves, and the small green or purplish flower clusters carry bent bristles. At maturity, the stem commonly breaks beneath the flower head, allowing it to move away from the parent plant. Plants may behave as annuals or persist longer, and closely related grasses can be difficult to separate.
identification: Look for an open, often drooping flower head, narrow leaves and tiny bent awns. Mature heads may break away; a botanical key is needed for close relatives.
actions: Photograph mature flower heads and basal growth for identification. Check regional status before removal, since this grass is native in parts of its range.

proposedDescription: Bermuda buttercup is a bulb-forming perennial from southern Africa, with bright yellow flowers held above a loose cluster of leaves. Each leaf has three heart-shaped leaflets, often dotted with purple. Despite its common name, it is a wood sorrel rather than a true buttercup. In California it grows during the cooler, wetter part of the year and retreats to underground bulbs as weather warms. Those bulbs allow patches to return and can spread the plant when contaminated soil is moved.
identification: Look for three heart-shaped leaflets, clustered yellow flowers on leafless stalks and small underground bulbs. Distinguish it from low, creeping wood sorrels.
actions: Avoid moving soil from infested patches. Where removal is appropriate, collect bulbs carefully and revisit the area, since cutting off leaves alone leaves bulbs alive.
researchNotes: UC's California biology is kept regional; the same article includes O. corniculata, whose seed-based spread and management were not transferred. Kew-hosted Flora of Iraq is independently authored and supports bulb reproduction and southern African range. No claim that the species never produces viable seed worldwide.

proposedDescription: Bermudagrass is a low, wiry perennial grass that grows most actively in warm weather. It spreads through runners above ground and underground stems, both able to root and form new plants. Narrow leaves and fingerlike branches radiating from the tip of each flower stalk help distinguish a flowering patch. It is widely grown as turf, yet the same spreading growth makes it a persistent weed in gardens and planting beds. In cooler conditions the foliage turns brown as the grass becomes dormant.
identification: Check for rooting runners, underground stems, a fringe of white hairs where leaf meets sheath and three to seven fingerlike flower-head branches.
actions: Keep runners and contaminated soil out of beds where it is unwanted. Remove spreading stems repeatedly and monitor regrowth; fragments left in moist soil can root.

proposedDescription: Bhutan pine is an evergreen mountain tree from the Himalayan region, also known as Himalayan pine. Its long, gray-green needles grow in bundles of five and hang downward on older shoots, giving the branches a soft, drooping appearance. Long, resinous cones hang from stalks, while bark changes from smooth gray-green on young wood to darker, fissured scales with age. The species is grown as an ornamental beyond its native range and generally favors sunny sites with well-drained soil.
identification: Count five needles per bundle and look for long, drooping needles and long-stalked, resinous cones. Compare mature cones with other five-needle pines.
actions: Document needles, cones and overall form to confirm identification. Assess local planting or naturalization status before deciding whether any management is needed.
researchNotes: Oregon State horticultural observations and Kew/WCVP are independent sources. Common name Bhutan pine refers here to P. wallichiana; no claim about P. bhutanica. proposedDescription: Bicolored trailing ants are tiny, shiny ants with a dark head and abdomen contrasting with a much lighter middle section. Workers are less than two millimeters long and often forage on trees, shrubs and around buildings in warm climates. Colonies occupy small cavities, including spaces in twigs and bark, and may contain several queens. The ants take insects and sweet foods, including honeydew from plant-feeding bugs. Their small nests can travel with nursery plants and other material moved by people.
identification: Use magnification to check the dark head and abdomen, pale middle and two-part waist. Confirm a collected specimen because other small household ants can look similar.
actions: Inspect nursery plants and small cavities before moving them. Indoors, remove accessible food and seek species identification before selecting a targeted control.

proposedDescription: Mouse-ear chickweed is a low, spreading perennial with small paired leaves and white flowers. Its softly hairy growth can blend into lawns until the flowers appear, each with five notched petals. Originally from Europe, it now grows widely in North America in fields, roadsides and other open, disturbed places. The flowers are small, with petals about as long as the green sepals beneath them. Those details help separate it from similar chickweeds.
identification: Look for opposite, untoothed leaves and small white flowers; compare petal length with the sepals before identifying it.

proposedDescription: Large quaking grass has flower clusters that hang like little paper lanterns from fine stalks. The overlapping scales can turn brown or purple, and the loose clusters give this annual grass its distinctive nodding look. Native to the Mediterranean region, it grows in disturbed ground and has become established beyond its original range. Narrow, flat leaves form loose tufts beneath the flower stems. Its conspicuous clusters make it easier to recognize than many grasses.
identification: Look for relatively large, drooping oval flower clusters on threadlike stalks, with broad overlapping scales.

proposedDescription: Bighead carp are large freshwater fish with oversized heads, low-set eyes and irregular dark blotches along their bodies. proposedDescription: Bigheaded ants get their name from the unusually large heads of their larger workers, which forage alongside many smaller ants. actions: Seek identification before treating. For an established infestation, coordinate with neighboring properties and use locally approved bait or professional guidance.

proposedDescription: Birch leafminer is a small sawfly whose young feed between the upper and lower surfaces of birch leaves. proposedDescription: Black carpet beetles are small, dark, oval beetles whose young have a very different appearance and appetite. The narrow, brown, hairy larvae carry a long tuft at the rear and feed on wool, fur, feathers and other animal materials. Adults visit flowers for pollen and nectar and may enter buildings to lay eggs. Indoors, larvae can remain hidden in lint, stored textiles or insect collections; shed skins and irregular damage are often easier to find than the beetles themselves.

Eggs spend the winter on cherry twigs, while later generations commonly move to plants in the mustard family for summer. Lady beetles, lacewings and other predators help limit their numbers in orchards.

proposedDescription: Black poui, better known in many places as jacaranda, is a South American tree grown for its blue-purple flowers and fine, fern-like foliage. Its spreading branches create light shade, and the flowers can form a colorful carpet beneath the canopy. Rounded, woody seed capsules persist after flowering. It does best in warm conditions with sunshine and well-drained soil; frost limits where it can thrive. Its presence as a planted ornamental should be distinguished from evidence that it has escaped cultivation.
